#6681. Dua Lipa Has Already Got Her Hands on Winter’s Next It Coat

There is a certain kind of winter coat that’s popular right now. Dua Lipa, a longtime devotee of the fabulous, fantastical coat, understands this better than most. It’s one that requires very little else of its wearer. No elaborate styling or carefully coordinated separates needed. Just throw it on over a pair of jeans, and you're dressed. The coat is the outfit!

And so the singer has offered a first look at a yet-to-be-released piece from London-based designer Charlotte Simone’s forthcoming Winter Drop 2. The jacket features an enormous, shaggy brown collar, extravagant furry cuffs, and a cropped silhouette. Lipa wore hers with faded blue Icon Denim Didy jeans and a black Bottega Veneta Madison shoulder bag, allowing the outerwear to take center stage.

“Dua is a dream girl,” Simone tells Vogue. "She never looks overdone or precious about what she’s wearing. She’ll throw one of our coats over a simple pair of jeans or a slip dress, and suddenly the coat is the whole look. That’s exactly how I design… I want every style to be the statement, the piece that makes you feel instantly put together the moment you step out the door.”

Certainly, the fantasy coat is having quite the moment. Jennifer Lawrence has been wandering around New York in a sumptuous chartreuse velvet robe by Colleen Allen; Carelli’s vintage-inflected, fur-trimmed coats have been dominating London streets; and Kendall Jenner and Hailey Bieber have both fallen for Conner Ives’s extraordinary embroidered silk robes with lavish furry collars and cuffs. Forget sensible or anonymous winter layers: This season, outerwear is an opportunity for a little theater, with unexpected colors or an excess of fluff.

But Charlotte Simone was doing the statement coat long before this latest wave of maximalist winter dressing. Founded by Charlotte Simone Beecham, the London-based label has spent the better part of a decade cultivating a devoted following for its nostalgic Penny Lane jackets, exaggerated faux-fur collars and cuffs, fuzzy textures, and playful proportions. Taylor Swift, Gigi Hadid, Charli XCX, and Lila Moss are among the famous fans who have fallen under its spell. So distinctive are the designs that they have become instantly recognizable on the street.

Lipa herself is something of a repeat customer. Just a few weeks ago, she stepped out in New York wearing the brand's inky blue-black, wonderfully fuzzy Lila jacket, styled with light-wash denim, chunky black Chrome Hearts boots, oversized sunglasses, and a Chanel bag. The formula was much the same, an otherwise straightforward outfit transformed by one gloriously tactile piece of outerwear.

Part of Charlotte Simone’s enduring appeal is its deliberate approach to production. Rather than churning out endless collections, the label operates through a handful of carefully considered, limited-edition drops each year. Designed in London and produced in small batches with an emphasis on quality and longevity, its most coveted styles routinely sell out within minutes. The first winter drop, released in October, was especially personal: conceived by Simone during early mornings nursing her newborn, it drew on the golden hues of dawn, the romance of winter mornings, and the optimism of new beginnings.

Now comes Drop 2, and Lipa has already provided a persuasive preview. “I love her confidence,” Simone says. “She doesn’t chase trends; she wears what she loves and makes it entirely her own, and that’s the spirit of Charlotte Simone.”

In an era of increasingly extravagant outerwear, Dua Lipa knows that the Charlotte Simone coat doesn’t demand that you dress up. It does the dressing up for you. Set your alarms for Drop 2!

#6679. These Cozy Shoes Are Too Chic to Keep Indoors

Slippers in public? These fashionable pairs make a convincing case.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

At this point, we’ve all probably accepted that slippers are no longer strictly house shoes. They’ve been part of our everyday wardrobes for years, and it’s hardly unusual to see someone wearing a fuzzy pair of slip-ons with jeans and a nice coat. What’s more interesting is how far brands have taken the idea lately. And honestly, some of these new styles are just really good shoes, slippers or not.

Take Ugg’s Western-inspired designs. Cowboy boots aren’t going anywhere, and the brand has found a way to bring that look into the comfortable footwear it’s known for. It’s a fun alternative to a traditional Western boot, especially if you want something a little more relaxed for everyday wear.

Brunch’s collaboration with Madhappy is another one worth knowing about. The two brands share co-founder Joshua Sitt, so the partnership makes sense, but the shoes themselves are what caught our attention. Made with colorful crochet and lined with shearling, they look like someone turned a chunky knit sweater into a slipper. And considering how much we love a good sweater this time of year, why shouldn’t our feet get a sweater of their own?

For Sitt, the idea of making slippers part of an everyday wardrobe has always been central to Brunch. “Originally, the entire concept for the brand was taking the hotel slipper product which is famously associated with vacation and travel, and bringing it into something you can wear every single day inside and outside of your home,” he tells ELLE.

You can see that thinking at work in the Madhappy collaboration. “The shoe itself morphs the comfort that both brands prioritize as well as the fashion pieces of both brands,” he says.

What’s particularly interesting is that this isn’t limited to brands you’d normally associate with slippers. Hunter, whose rain boots have been a wardrobe staple for years, has a cozy option of its own. Simkhai has entered the category, too, and Alo has a pair that feels especially fitting for the Pilates-to-coffee crowd. It’s a pretty good indication of just how much room there is to play with a shoe that used to be purely practical.

The styling is arguably the best part. A Western-inspired pair would look great with straight-leg jeans and a suede jacket, while a softer, more understated slipper can make tailored trousers and a wool coat feel less formal. You don’t need to rethink your wardrobe to wear them. In fact, that’s part of the appeal.

As Sitt points out, slippers haven’t exactly been the most considered purchase in our wardrobes. Ask people what pair they own, and “you’ll get some crickets,” he says. Or maybe they “stole a pair at a wedding.” No offense to wedding favors, but we think it’s time for an upgrade.

Whether you’re looking for an alternative to your usual boots or simply want a pair of slippers you won’t want to change out of before leaving the house, these are the styles worth a closer look. Shop our favorites below.

#6676. Inside the First Competition Between Historic Vintage Timepieces

Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.

In the automotive world, high-end cars have gone head-to-head since the early 1920s. Judges didn’t evaluate them based on their speed, though—in a Concours d’Élégance, the prize goes to the best-looking vehicles. The tradition continues today in picturesque sites around the world where collectors submit their often very high-end vintage, classic cars. Surprisingly, there has never been an event for vintage timepieces.

Aurel Bacs, the famous auctioneer whose longstanding association with Phillips has shaped the watch collecting world, endeavored to change that. “It began with a meeting where I said, ‘I have a dream,’” he said in a press release. For the very first iteration of this competition, Bacs and Phillips partnered with Swiss heavyweight Vacheron Constantin. They expected to receive maybe 100 to 200 submissions, but the jury was forced to whittle down 550 of them to 34 finalist watches, whose owners were flown out from across the world for the Concours held at the Hôtel Président in Geneva.

“It was the most beautiful evening in the field ever,” Bacs said. At the Hôtel Président, around 200 attendees gathered, along with a jury of 14 watch-industry experts including Bacs himself, Ben Clymer of Hodinkee, writer and historian Nick Foulkes, longtime watch journalist Roberta Naas, and others. Watches could only be submitted for consideration in one category (Chronographs, Métiers d’Art, Chronomètre Royal, Astronomical Complications, Multiple Complications, Design, and Chiming Mechanisms) and were judged based on nine criteria: authenticity, elegance, rarity, impact on the history of Vacheron Constantin and/or on watchmaking in general, provenance, technicality, métiers d’art (artistic crafts), state of preservation, and emotional dimension.

The jurors deliberated over several hours until the winners of the seven categories and a Best of Show were finally selected. Following a cocktail reception, everyone gathered on the lower floor of the Hôtel Président to see the results from the watch world’s first Concours d'Élégance.

The first category featured a smattering of some of the maison’s most important wristwatches, including a highly rare ref. 4072 in stainless steel from 1940. However, it was a yellow gold pocket-watch chronograph from 1929 that won the day. The result was such a surprise that the audience, intimately familiar with the historical importance of pocket watches, audibly gasped inside the room. It made me wonder if these old-fashioned timepieces could regain their lost position as the pinnacle of watch collecting. This piece certainly warranted the love it received: in excellent condition and featuring a white enamel dial with dual registers in an “up-down” configuration, it’s a beautiful timepiece.

This category celebrates handcrafts such as enameling and gem-setting, and it featured a smattering of truly spectacular pieces—mostly sub-40mm wristwatches in precious metals with wild cloisonné or Grand Feu champlevé enamel dials depicting landmasses or animals.

However, a stunning pocket watch set with blue sapphires throughout the bezel and Roman indices won out.

When an older American gentleman stepped on stage to collect his prize, he explained to a stunned crowd that not only had his great-grandfather, Dr. Otto von Frangeš, been given the watch by His Majesty Alexander I of Yugoslavia, its original owner, but that he wore it while sitting in the motorcade during the king’s assassination in France in 1934. Otto’s middle son, Nikola, eventually smuggled the watch out of Yugoslavia by sewing it into the lining of his wife’s jacket as they fled the Iron Curtain in the late 1940s.

In 1907, Vacheron launched the Chronomètre Royal sub-brand, specifically built to endure a life sailing the seas. The model’s parts were anti-magnetic and resisted rusting. The dials were made out of enamel, which could also stand up to the moist atmosphere without rusting. Because they were critical to maritime navigation, timing precision was of the utmost importance, and models from this line frequently won observatory trials (which tested for a watch’s accuracy) that ran from the 1800s to the mid-1900s. Given all that information, the winner is a bit of a shocker: a ref. 2215 from 1976 that exemplifies the qualities of the line but modernizes them in many ways. It doesn’t even feature a full set of numerals, trading them out for a few diamond-set indices. In his acceptance speech, the owner said he wears it on the weekends with jeans.

The Astronomical Complications category is dear to the heart of anyone who appreciates a good moonphase display and also includes timepieces equipped with a triple-calendar, a complete calendar, or a perpetual calendar. Though more modern pieces, such as a skeletonized QP wristwatch from 1987, made it to the final round, it was a wildly neat (and unique) platinum-cased “Cioccolatone” from 1957 that won out. Housed in a 34mm x 43mm rectangular case and equipped with a complete calendar, it’s owned by a dapper Italian collector, who beamed as he collected the prize with his grown son. This would not be this pair’s first time at the podium…

This is a loaded category for Vacheron, which famously makes the most complicated pocket watch and wristwatch in the world, with 57 and 41 complications, respectively. To be eligible in this category, watches were required to have at least two complications—child’s play for VC.

Spanning everything from an enamel-dialed, minute-repeating, split-seconds chronograph pocket watch from 1901 to several Patrimony watches from the 1990s, the winner was the “Don Pancho.” Delivered in 1940, this diminutive yellow-gold timepiece with minute repeater, day, and retrograde date indications was once the world’s most complicated wristwatch. Double-signed by Brooking in Madrid, it sold for roughly $740,000 at auction back in 2019.

A more subjective category, perhaps, than the others, Design included watches “featuring Vacheron Constantin’s signature design, either in the case or through the time display.” One entrant, for example—a wild time-only ref. 4695 dress watch—featured incredibly intricate lugs and a Maltese Cross-type dial. But the winner was nothing short of revelatory. Once again owned by the aforementioned tall Italian gentleman, the possibly unique ref. 6213 is an automatic world timer from 1957 in yellow gold. Based upon Louis Cottier’s famous system, it is so rare that even Clymer admitted he had never heard of it before the competition. The owner’s son described his father returning home with it one day when he was a boy, excited beyond belief that he had finally tracked it down after years of searching.

This category included pocket watches or wristwatches fitted with a minute repeater, quarter repeater, half-quarter repeater, or grand sonnerie—a mechanism that automatically strikes the hours and quarter-hours every 15 minutes. Incredibly, among the entrants was a red gold quarter-repeater pocket watch from the early 1820s with a stunning guilloché dial. However, the winner was another pocket watch dating to 1926 and cased in platinum. Its ultra-thin design, black Breguet numerals, Breguet blued steel handset, and simple silver dial belied the complex mechanism within. The visibly emotional American gentleman who owns it recalled how, as a boy, he would open a chest of drawers, remove his grandfather’s pocket watch, and listen to its minute repeater.

A bonus category, Best of Show went to a truly spectacular wristwatch: a ref. 6448 in platinum with diamond-set indices. Seemingly a simple time-only dress watch, this tremendous piece—which was produced in just three examples in the early 1960s—boasts a hand-wound, 13-ligne minute-repeater movement. Housed in a brushed-finish case with incredible teardrop lugs, it’s the only known example in this metal, and it was notably the last minute-repeating reference produced by the brand for nearly 30 years.

Nominally, the crowd at the awards ceremony was there to judge the merits of a watch, but I left emotionally moved by the stories each watch owner shared about their timepieces. As the very first concours for watches, the format will no doubt be repeated in the future—either by Vacheron, adopted by other brands, or done as a more traditional multi-brand event like the Concours d’Élégance at Pebble Beach.

In recent years, press tours have become even buzzier than whatever’s being promoted. Not that we’re complaining—we were first in line to gush over the array of bright pink outfits Margot Robbie wore throughout her 2023 press appearances for Barbie, and again earlier this year when the actor was promoting Wuthering Heights, gracing our social feeds with enviable corsetry reminiscent of her character, Cathy.

As for another scene-stealing star who knows how to turn a look, Daisy Edgar-Jones has been out in force in a mixture of casual and formal outfits to promote her latest on-screen endeavor, Sense and Sensibility. Styled by Dani Michelle, Edgar-Jones has been on a run of wearing some of the most buzzy luxury labels, including Prada, Chloé, and Schiaparelli.

But this time, it’s not the statement pieces we’ve got our eye on. Instead, a humble pair of jeans.

Known for her love of vintage Levi’s, Edgar-Jones has been photographed wearing the same pair of straight, cropped jeans on two occasions during this ongoing press tour. Styling them on the first outing with an archive Galliano top with a cinched waist and blossoming collar, she finished the look with a Boucheron choker and gold peep-toe heels. #6673. Women’s Sports Teams Deserve Better Than What Their Homes Are Giving Them

Apparently, we’re going through this...again!

Gotham FC, the current reigning National Women’s Soccer Team champions, are on their way to winning another title. But their journey—which includes the chance to host their first semifinal game at home—has come with a major surprise: a change of venues. After their quarterfinal match against the Seattle Reign FC ended with a messed-up pitch and a fine against Gotham FC due to its conditions, the team was forced to find another place for their next match. The bigger issue? Their only option is a 5,000-person stadium located in Randall’s Island, New York.

Over 11,000 people made their way to Sports Illustrated Stadium—the home to Gotham FC as well as the MLS’s New York Red Bulls—to see them take down Seattle Reign FC. This means that less than half of that audience will be able to catch them at the match that can lead them to the finals.

While pitch conditions are absolutely important for the safety of the players and a big enough reason to change venues, the option to upgrade the pitch to a hybrid model was shut down by none other than New York Red Bulls due to a friendly game—AKA a game that does not count towards their season—they have on Saturday. Although the pitch would be ready for Gotham FC’s big game, RBNY shut down the plan as it wouldn’t be ready for their planned friendly. All of a sudden, a game-making match for a winning women’s team was being moved to a much smaller space due to a men’s game that does not count towards anything.

If you’re getting a sense of deja vu, that’s because this is not the first time a women’s team had to change their plans due to a men’s team. The WNBA’s Atlanta Dream were forced to move one of their WNBA Finals games from 8 p.m. to 12:30 p.m. on a Thursday. While the move was caused by them switching venues—going from their home at the Gateway Center, which fits 3,500 to the State Farm Arena which seats 17,000—it was also caused by a scheduled Atlanta Hawks game, a team that hasn’t won an NBA title since the 1950s.

It’s clear that no matter where they go, these women’s teams’ homes are not giving them what they need: a space where they can continue to host their ever-growing fanbases without fear of having to fall to the needs of a men’s team. The WNBA had a 21 percent increase in attendance to their games in 2026. The NWSL also gained some new faces in the crowd with a 3 percent increase, according to Sports Business Journal.

In 2028, Gotham FC will move to Etihad Park, a new stadium that will hold 25,000 fans in Queens, NYC. However, they’ll still have the problem of sharing the field with New York City FC, meaning this problem can always come up again.

A clear solution would be to give these incredible teams their own venues, but it’s evident that, financially, building a new stadium is not the easiest for some of these teams who are still growing. But, maybe next time, these men’s teams will just get the hint and let the real winners take over. It’s their home, too, after all.

#6672. Rosalía Wins With Her Style at the 2026 Latin Grammy Awards

She wore a quartet of designer looks from Matières Fécales, Erdem, Vivienne Westwood, and Dior

Rosalía won big at the 27th annual Latin Grammy Awards last night. For her fourth studio album, Lux, the Spanish pop singer took home her third trophy for Album of the Year, becoming the first woman in the history of the ceremony to ever do so. She collected a total of five awards, coming out on top in other major categories like Song of the Year, which was awarded to her track “La Perla” (featuring Yahritza y Su Esencia), and Best Short Form Music Video, which went to her visual for “Sauvignon Blanc.” And to coincide with such a major night, Rosalía brought out a few major designer looks, all styled by Chloe & Chenelle Delgadillo.

To start the evening, the “Berghain” singer hit the red carpet in the avant-garde label of the moment, Matières Fécales, which has been embraced by everyone from Zendaya to Rihanna and Demi Moore.

Courtesy of the label’s Spring/Summer 2027 collection, Rosalía’s angelic white gown featured a ruched tulle bodice with semi-sheer folds that hugged her body and culminated in the house’s signature déchiré detailing. The tattered fragments arched from Rosalía’s shoulders like wings, while also dangling from the ends of her cropped sleeves. Down low, there was equal drama courtesy of a dramatic tulle bubble skirt that trailed around her in a voluminous cascade. Of course, her signature halo-dyed hair acted as the perfect complement to the heavenly ensemble.

Later, Rosalía hit the stage to perform a medley of songs from Lux, including “La Perla,” “La Rumba del Perdón,” and “Dios Es un Stalker.” For her performance, she wore a bespoke satin gown from Erdem, pulled from the house’s Fall/Winter 2026 collection. (Just last month, she turned to the same London-based label for a stunning balletcore street-style moment.)

The golden-hued design featured a corset-style bodice and knotted bows along the neckline, with a basque waist and flared ruffle skirt that was overlayed with black tulle and trimmed with ostrich feathers.

Once she returned to her seat, it turned out Rosalía had another surprise look in store, as she changed into a custom white dress from Vivienne Westwood. The bridal-inspired design featured a strapless, plunging sweetheart bodice decorated with a tiny bow in the middle, while layers of fabric were draped along the waist for a subtle peplum effect.

All of the fabric, meanwhile, was embroidered with floral lace details and microscopic pearl embellishments, and the singer wore a scarf to match, while slipping into a pair of contrasting black pumps.

To finish her quartet of looks, Rosalía switched into a custom black Dior dress by Jonathan Anderson, who, fittingly, also helped design many of the looks for the Spanish superstar’s recent Lux Tour.

The silky black slip featured two delicate lace straps that hung off Rosalía’s shoulders, while the bust tied into a knot that dangled in front like a tassel. The top half of the dress was decorated with subtle floral details, while the skirt featured panels of semi-sheer material. It all worked perfectly to serve as an inky backdrop as Rosalía posed with her stack of gramophone trophies.

As she accepted her prize for Album of the Year, Rosalía got teary-eyed, saying: “This is the third time I’ve won this award. If El Mal Querer was a dream, and Motomami was a bold gamble, then Lux has been a leap into the unknown. I believe it’s very important to speak your own truth—and for others to be able to speak theirs—and this record is mine. I thank God, and I thank my loved ones: my family and my friends. Thank you for your love and for shaping me into who I am today. The truth is, I know I still have a lot to learn, and I’m certain that I likely haven’t even created my best work yet.”

#6671. The Benefits of Sauna Therapy: What to Know Before You Sweat

Experts explain how sauna sessions may support circulation, recovery, skin health, and stress relief.

Although saunas may not be the most relaxing spa or high-end gym amenity, recent studies show that as little as 30 minutes in a hot box can significantly boost the immune system and reduce the risk of cardiovascular and mental health issues, including hypertension and dementia. A physician should monitor the practice, particularly if you have any preexisting conditions. Sauna sessions can also offer several beauty benefits. The research reveals that quick stints in high heat are just enough to jump-start stress reduction, help fight off a cold, and even give skin a nice little glow-up. Experts break down the perks of sauna therapy and how to do it safely.

According to board-certified surgeon, physician, and longevity specialist Dr. Darshan Shah, who is also the founder and CEO of Next Health, sauna therapy offers several potential benefits for both physical and mental well-being, including:

Muscle Recovery: Increased blood flow helps deliver oxygen and nutrients to muscle tissue, supporting recovery and relieving muscle tension.

Skin Rejuvenation: Increased circulation helps deliver oxygen and nutrients to the skin, supporting a healthy-looking complexion. Heat exposure may also support skin health and collagen production, which plays an important role in maintaining skin elasticity and firmness.

Immunity & Cardiovascular Health: Heat exposure raises core body temperature, supporting the body’s natural immune response, while promoting vasodilation and improved circulation. Regular sauna use may also help support healthy blood pressure and vascular function.

Weight Management: Heat exposure temporarily increases heart rate and energy expenditure—although he clarifies that sweating primarily results in water loss rather than fat loss.

Detoxification: Sweating helps the body eliminate small amounts of certain substances, while heat exposure may also support circulation and lymphatic function.

There’s a difference, but it’s worth noting that the aforementioned study and conclusions gathered from it focused on dry heat. However, Shah says the main difference is how the heat is delivered and how your body responds to each.

Brianna Olamiju, a board-certified dermatologist at Spring Street Dermatology in NYC, adds that the benefits of dry saunas and steam rooms are similar, including increased circulation and relaxation. “Dry saunas typically operate at higher temperatures with lower humidity, while steam rooms have lower temperatures and significantly higher humidity,” she explains. Steam rooms may temporarily relieve nasal congestion, but Olamiju shares that neither has been proven superior for skin health. “People with sensitive skin, eczema, or rosacea may find that excessive heat aggravates their symptoms,” she tells ELLE.

Shah’s take is that ultimately, the best option depends on personal preference, heat tolerance, and individual wellness goals. “Consistency and finding an approach that feels comfortable are more important than choosing one type of sauna over another.”

Traditional dry saunas typically operate between 150°F and 195°F, while steam rooms are generally around 100°F to 120°F. Olamiju explains that although many studies have examined sauna benefits at approximately 175°F, she says there is no universally established ideal temperature. “I recommend starting at a comfortable temperature and gradually increasing as tolerated. Higher temperatures don’t necessarily translate to greater benefits,” says Olamiju.

Temperature matters when determining the intensity of heat exposure and how your body responds. Shah concurs that hotter doesn’t necessarily mean better. “The goal is to find a temperature that allows you to experience the benefits of heat exposure without putting unnecessary stress on your body,” he adds.

Another option that Shah’s Next Health saunas utilize is infrared heat. These chambers operate between 110°F and 140°F. “Unlike traditional saunas, which can reach significantly higher temperatures, infrared technology uses light-based heat to warm the body directly. This creates a more tolerable experience for many individuals and can allow for longer sessions,” Shah explains.

Studies show that dry air at high temperatures (typically 70 to 100 °C) for 10 to 30 minutes per session was the sweet spot to reap some of the more significant benefits of sauna therapy, but Shah says there is no one-size-fits-all number since the frequency of infrared sauna use will vary depending on individual factors such as health goals, tolerance, and time constraints. “As a starting point, I generally recommend a client aim for two to three sessions per week for maximized benefits,” says Shah.

For beginners, Olamiju suggests starting with five to 10 minutes per session and gradually increasing to 15 to 20 minutes as tolerated. Two to three sessions per week are recommended as a reasonable starting point. “Some studies suggest that more frequent sauna use may be associated with greater cardiovascular benefits, but consistency and individual tolerance are most important,” Olamiju also notes.

Both experts agree that a wide range of individuals can benefit. For Olamiju, it’s anyone looking to reduce stress, improve relaxation, or relieve muscle soreness. “It may also offer cardiovascular benefits for some individuals. However, sauna therapy should complement, rather than replace, regular exercise and other healthy lifestyle habits,” she advises.

Shah says sauna therapy is particularly useful for those looking to support circulation, recovery, skin health, and overall well-being. He adds that if you’re experiencing chronic pain or muscle tension, a sauna session can help, as increased blood flow may help alleviate discomfort and support recovery. Lastly, he says sauna therapy may also support skin health by promoting collagen production, which can improve skin elasticity and contribute to a smoother, more radiant complexion. “Overall, sauna therapy may be particularly appealing to individuals looking to manage everyday aches and pains, support skin rejuvenation, improve circulation, or simply incorporate more relaxation and recovery into their wellness routines,” says Shah.

Like any form of heat therapy, sauna use isn’t appropriate for everyone, and it’s important to understand your individual health considerations. “Individuals with cardiovascular conditions, uncontrolled blood pressure, a history of fainting, or other underlying health concerns should consult their physician before starting sauna therapy. Pregnant individuals should also seek medical guidance before using a sauna,” Shah warns.

Some of the biggest risks of sauna therapy are dehydration, overheating, dizziness, and low blood pressure, so stay hydrated before, during, and after your sessions. From a dermatologic perspective, Olamiju also explains that excessive heat and sweating can exacerbate conditions like rosacea, eczema, and sensitive skin. “I recommend staying hydrated, rinsing off after sauna sessions, and applying moisturizer to support the skin barrier,” she says.

Can older individuals reap the benefits of sauna therapy?

Absolutely. But both Shah and Olamiju warn that age can bring changes in cardiovascular function, blood pressure regulation, and the body’s ability to manage heat. If you’re taking medications that affect blood pressure or hydration, consult your physician before beginning sauna therapy. Also, start with shorter sessions at lower temperatures and gradually adjust based on comfort and tolerance. “The goal isn’t to achieve a particular temperature or duration; it’s to find a safe, sustainable routine that supports long-term health and quality of life,” says Shah.

#6667. FKA Twigs’s Josephine Baker Transformation Is Already a Beauty Spectacle

With lacquered curls spiraling across her forehead, a dark and smoky gaze, and a megawatt smile, FKA twigs has all but disappeared into Josephine Baker. The first image of the British musician as the legendary entertainer in the forthcoming biopic Josephine Baker has arrived, and if this is anything to go by, we’re in for an on-screen beauty transformation for the ages.

In the image, twigs stands atop a dining table, twisting into a playful pose in a pink, crystal-strewn flapper dress with delicate beading and fringe. But it’s the beauty that really transports us to 1920s Paris. Her hair has been molded into an ultra-glossy, close-cropped style, with elaborate kiss curls arranged across her forehead and temples. Her eyes are rimmed with smoldering shadow, her brows sharply defined, and her lips painted a rich red. It’s classic Baker, down to the mischievous expression.

After all, few performers have left such an enduring mark on beauty history. Baker’s signature Eton crop, sculpted finger waves, and intricate S-shaped kiss curls helped define the Jazz Age. She understood the transformative potential of hair and makeup: brows drawn into fine, expressive arches, heavily kohled eyes, and dark, precisely shaped lips. Hers was a highly theatrical, unapologetically glamorous approach to beauty, one that challenged conventional standards and continues to inform red-carpet trends a century later.

You need only look at the recent Met Galas for proof. At the 2025 event, Baker’s influence was everywhere: Dua Lipa, Sydney Sweeney, and Coco Jones were among those sporting intricate forehead curls, while Gigi Hadid and twigs herself paid tribute to the entertainer through their clothing. The following year, the kiss curl remained a red-carpet fixture, appearing in elaborate interpretations on Lisa and Kylie Jenner. Elsewhere, Ayo Edebiri, Odessa A’zion, and Chappell Roan have all experimented with variations of the look in 2026.

A fellow dancer, singer, and consummate performer, twigs has long treated beauty as an extension of her artistic expression, experimenting with sculptural hairstyles and otherworldly makeup. Baker was celebrated for an exuberant, often comedic stage persona, finding ways to subvert the expectations and racial stereotypes imposed upon her. Their aesthetics aren’t identical—twigs gravitates toward the experimental and occasionally surreal, where Baker delighted in humor and Jazz Age showmanship—but both understand the power of a carefully constructed image.

Indeed, twigs has already explored Baker’s beauty codes. At the 2025 Met Gala, she wore an ultra-short Eton crop and a Josephine-inspired feathered dress by Grace Wales Bonner. Speaking to Vogue at the time, she described Baker, alongside Eartha Kitt and Grace Jones, as an embodiment of female dandyism. The admiration clearly runs deep.

The forthcoming film, directed by Maïmouna Doucouré, will follow Baker’s extraordinary life from her ascent to stardom in 1920s Paris through her work with the French Resistance during World War II and her involvement in the American civil rights movement. Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor stars as Baker’s mother, with the production spanning multiple decades and locations. Filming reportedly began this fall.

The project marks the first major screen adaptation of the Baker’s life and has received the full blessing of the late singer’s estate. “She lives on in our hearts as a visionary, ground-breaking woman whose story is as powerful as it is relevant today,” twigs said in a press statement.

The expansive timeline offers a sweeping beauty playground for lead makeup artist Laura Ozier, working alongside costume designer Emmanuelle Youchnovski, whose credits include The Substance. Beyond the early kiss curls, we’ll see Baker’s sleek side-parted bob, gelled head, and 1940s coiffures, 1950s updos, plus some very dramatic on-stage makeup. Expect some enormous feathered headdresses and glitter decals that became part of her later performance wardrobe. We’ll also surely see the more restrained side of Baker away from the spotlight, as her life took her from cabaret stages into wartime resistance and political activism.

Baker’s appearance evolved alongside her ambitions and her growing cultural influence. For FKA twigs, whose own career has been defined by artistic reinvention, the opportunity is enormous. And judging by this first glimpse, the beauty alone will be worth watching for.

#6666. How This Flexible Balm Foundation Held Up to My 12-Hour Day

The skin care-enhanced formula glides on easily and doesn’t quit.

As a mom in my 40s, I ask a lot of my foundation. I have less time to spend in front of the mirror, yet my skin demands more attention: There are acne scars, hyperpigmentation, and redness to cover, plus dryness that makes it tricky to blend makeup seamlessly. Heavy foundations can easily settle into my fine lines, emphasize my pores, and mute my glow. I need a foundation that’s hydrating yet lightweight, with coverage that’s buildable and easy to touch up during long days.

Unfortunately, not many foundations check all of these boxes. I know this firsthand: I’ve been writing about beauty products for more than 15 years and have tested most of the popular options out there. Few seem designed with mature skin in mind, and most tend to become cakey and dry, especially during midday touch-ups.

But L’Oréal Paris True Match Hyaluron Tinted Balm Foundation fits the bill. It’s made using 80 percent skin care ingredients, including skin-plumping hyaluronic acid. That helps the formula hydrate and smooth skin while also minimizing fine lines and wrinkles over time. Here’s my detailed review of how this foundation looked and felt from morning until night.

I tested the Tinted Balm Foundation ahead of a long, meeting-packed weekday. Using the included teardrop-shaped sponge applicator, I applied and blended from the center of my face outward. The narrow tip let me precisely target the corners of my nose and my dark under-eye circles, and build coverage, so I didn’t need concealer. Then, as I blended the foundation across my cheeks and forehead, it melted right in for that elusive second-skin finish.

One thing I noticed right away: This foundation’s luminous tinted-balm texture is unique, in a good way. It sank into my skin for effortless blending and was so lightweight and breathable that I even felt comfortable using it on my chin, which is prone to hormonal acne thanks to perimenopause. Boosting radiance at a time when my skin has been growing more dry and dull, it also blurred imperfections, including the hard-to-cover redness around my nose and melasma on my forehead.

The foundation comes in a neat mirrored compact, which is much more convenient for on-the-go touch-ups than a messy bottle or tube. After applying it, I tucked it into my crossbody pouch before heading out.

I applied my foundation around 7 A.M. to see how it held up during a 12-hour day of working, exercising, carpooling, and socializing. The verdict: This is one foundation that can actually keep up with a woman over 40—and meet her skin needs.

Mid-morning: The first challenge of the day involved walking my dog around the neighborhood. I live on the coast of Maine, where the weather changes by the hour. The wind and salty mist did a number on my blowout, but my foundation still looked freshly applied and flawless when I checked it prior to a 9:30 A.M. video call for work.

Late morning: My foundation was still going strong at 11 A.M., when I hit the gym. Afterward, I slid the compact out for a quick touch-up, mostly reapplying around my nose and covering a couple of chin pimples. I appreciate that the sponge applicator is antimicrobial, which helps prevent bacteria from exacerbating my acne.

Mid-afternoon: Around 3 P.M., after hours at my laptop, I left to cheer my daughters on in back-to-back high school soccer games. This is the time of day when foundation can start to look tired, especially on mature skin. I snuck out the compact for a quick face check. My foundation had not settled into my crow’s feet, and my skin still looked and felt hydrated and comfortable, not parched. A quick touch-up of my dark circles was all it took to keep my makeup looking on point.

Evening: I arrived home around 8:30 P.M., ate a quick dinner with my family, then did one final complexion inspection before showering. After a long day, including many hours out in the elements and two quick foundation touch-ups, my skin still looked fresh and even.

I’d recommend L’Oréal Paris True Match Hylauron Tinted Balm Foundation to any friends over 40 looking for an easygoing foundation that hydrates, minimizes imperfections, and boosts glow. The skin care-enhanced formula and convenient compact make this a top pick for anyone juggling the busy schedules and skin concerns that come with middle age.

For all-day comfort, what should you look for in a foundation for mature skin?

To nurture mature skin, look for a foundation that incorporates skin care ingredients such as hyaluronic acid, which helps hydrate and plump skin and ensures smooth application. The formula should be lightweight and buildable enough to cover imperfections without feeling heavy or settling into fine lines.

How can you reapply foundation without it looking cakey?

Start by choosing a lightweight foundation that’s hydrating and buildable, such as L’Oréal Paris True Match Hyaluron Tinted Balm Foundation, and apply it in thin layers. Then, for touch-ups, use the teardrop sponge applicator to precisely dab and blend makeup just where needed, like around the nose or directly onto blemishes and hyperpigmentation.

#6664. JFK Jr.’s ’94 Saab Is Up for Auction. You Should Buy It

The late John F. Kennedy Jr., in addition to being the subject of countless menswear moodboards, a hit Ryan Murphy series, and, hey, a new coffee table book written by yours truly, was one of the most stylish guys in 1990s New York. Between his American-dynasty pedigree, chiseled good looks, and impossibly thick head of hair, not to mention his eclectic wardrobe of preppy classics, funky gorpcore, and Armani suits, it’s not hard to see why. It should come as no surprise, then, that he also had excellent taste in cars. Throughout the ’90s, JFK Jr.’s whip of choice was a 1994 Saab 900 SE Coupe, a quirky Swedish sports car that embodied everything that was great about ’90s style, down to its hunter green paint. Fortunately, for fans of oddball vintage autos and JFK Jr. alike, it’s currently up for sale via RR Auction, and the bids are rolling in.

Sporty, sophisticated, and eccentric, the Saab 900 was to JFK Jr. what the pink Cadillac Fleetwood was to Elvis, or the Porsche 935 was to Paul Newman. An consummate outlier in the American car market since the ’50s, Saab’s popularity peaked in the mid-1980s when its weird, angular designs and quirks(e.g., the ignition was next to the handbrake) found a following among design-obsessed American yuppies. Combining the Scandinavian sobriety of a Volvo with the postmodern flair of a Memphis sofa, Saab loomed large in ’90s culture: Jerry Seinfeld’s TV alter-ego drove one, as did Niles Crane, Dana Scully, and Clark Griswald’s humorless neighbors in National Lampoon’s Christmas Vacation.

During the tail end of the decade, when JFK Jr. and his late wife, publicist Carolyn Bessette Kennedy, were fixtures of Lower Manhattan life, the couple was frequently photographed driving in the Saab near their Tribeca loft. With its sporty-yet-economical turbocharged four-cylinder engine, a sleek leather interior, and a custom set of aftermarket aqua-blue padded ski racks mounted to the roof, it embodied JFK Jr.’s characteristic blend of aristocratic, athletic, and bohemian to a tee.

JFK Jr.'s green 1994 Saab 900 SE, with a current bid of nearly $30,000 and rising.

According to Bobby Livingston, executive vice president at RR Auction, “what makes this lot so special is it's not some Maserati or something flashy like that—it's a practical car that was a part of his everyday life. For Kennedy, “the choice of this car, as opposed to a Mercedes or something, speaks a lot to his style.” This particular Saab—which JFK Jr. purchased new from Zumbach Sports Cars in Manhattan for $29,841.21 in the summer of 1994, and owned until his death in 1999—comes to auction via Kevin J. Hynes, a screenwriter and longtime friend of Kennedy’s who worked with him at the New York DA’s office in the early ’90s. According to the auction listing, the car had been left at Hynes’s Westchester home in the days following Kennedy’s fatal plane crash. In 2000, Hynes then bought the car from the Kennedy estate in 2000 for $6,000, and sold it for $12,000 two years later. Its third owner is said to have started up the car regularly, but judging by its overall condition and the looks of its odometer, which shows just 30,650 miles, it seems it hasn’t hit the road in a long time.

The Saab, which was listed with a minimum sale price of $15,000, is part of a RR’s Fine Autographs and Artifacts auction that also includes a tweed hat worn by the elder JFK and Lee Harvey Oswald’s overcoat. As of Wednesday afternoon, more than 20 bids have driven the price close to $30,000. “We’ve sold a Hummer that belonged to Tupac, and a Cadillac Escalade that was used by Tony Soprano in The Sopranos, but I didn't know there would be such an affection for John F. Kennedy Jr.’s Saab,” says Livingston. “It’s already exceeded our estimate, and there’s a lot of interest, so it could go for a lot more than where it is right now.”

The Kennedys, seen here in 1998, were frequently seen driving in the Saab near their Tribeca loft.

Given its provenance and climbing auction price tag, whether JFK Jr.’s Saab ends up with a car collector, a Kennedy buff, or someone with a keen appreciation for peak-1990s style, one hopes that whoever buys it will be well-equipped to give it the treatment it deserves. That is to say, this is a car that deserves to be street-parked in Tribeca, driven to Vermont for ski trips, and otherwise treated like the ’90s style icon it is. A backward Kangol cap and an “I TOLD YA” tee are optional, but highly recommended.

#6663. I Found the Most Comfortable Pointed-Toe Boots

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Buying pointed-toe boots has always been a challenge for me because I’m built like a ballerina—not, sadly, in terms of long legs or elegant arms or a swanlike neck, but in terms of feet. I have the bunions of a woman who has dedicated her life to the art of dance, which is ironic because I took ballet lessons for all of three months when I was eight. (I quit after they let me wear the tutu, which was really the only thing I was in it for.) I am confessing this not because I enjoy talking about my feet on the internet, but to establish my credibility when I say that I have finally found a pair of slim, sexy, pointed-toe boots that are comfortable enough to wear all day, even for those of us with less-than-ideal extremities.

Margaux’s Inga boots have a long, squared-off toe and a little kitten heel that measures 1.5 inches—tall enough to give you a bit of a lift, but low enough to be walkable. They come in black leather and a sleek espresso suede, both of which look great with jeans but would also be cute peeking out of long, drapey trousers. The best part is the sizing: Margaux offers its boots in narrow, medium, and wide, and somehow, through the magic of proportion play, the wide does not look wide. They accommodate the fullest part of my foot without looking bulky or breaking up the nice long line.

The first time I wore them, it was to a witches’ dinner that my friend Mo throws every Halloween. She invites 30 of her best female friends over, decorates her home in high goth style, and serves us a theatrically witchy meal. (This time, it was black squid-ink pasta.) Of course, one has to dress appropriately to dine with the coven, so I paired the boots with slim black jeans and a sheer black polka-dotted top. Not only did I get a bunch of compliments, but I didn’t find myself pining for my broomstick on the walk home—the boots were just as comfortable at the end of the evening as they’d been at the start of the night.

They’ve held up equally well on the commute to work. In addition to the extra width, they also come with five millimeters of cushioning on the inside, which is enough to protect you when you’re pounding the pavement. Ever since slimmer toes reentered the fashion conversation, I’ve been faced with the choice between sitting out the trend or hobbling around in boots that fundamentally do not fit. As much as I love a good pair of shoes, I also live for a long walk, and the Ingas, miraculously, let me have both. Really, they don’t feel like heels at all, which is a rare and wonderful thing for a pair of pointed-toe kitten-heel boots.

#6662. Restaurant Booths Are Back—and Better Than Ever

“When I walk into a restaurant and see a worn-in bright red-and-white striped booth, I already know it’s going to be good,” says Anna Albury, designer and writer behind Cool Stuff NYC, the cult-followed newsletter she curates with her husband, Garrett. She, like many booth loyalists, can wax poetic about her favorite seats in the city, citing the coat-rack-clad booths of Cobble Hill’s Long Island Bar, Le Veau d’Or’s cherry-red banquettes on the Upper East Side, and Carroll Gardens newcomer Trudie’s, which features charming two-top booths.

While booths have long been considered the “best seat in the house,” there was a time in the not-so-distant past when business diners preferred private dining rooms and social diners sought out communal tables. But there’s good news for booth lovers like Albury: this past year has brought on a booth boom of never-before-seen proportions. Restaurants, hotels, and members’ clubs of all distinctions are installing booths and banquettes by the mile. From design-forward diners like London-based Supernova to fine dining institutions like the Roman and Williams–designed Marcel and swanky cocktail lounges like Andres Diaz’s newly opened Bar Leone, without a doubt, booths are back.

Mohair-upholstered booths are a key feature of the newly opened Marcel restaurant in New York, designed by Roman and Williams.

Interior designers who cater to hospitality venues are seeing the shift in demand firsthand. “Across daytime and evening-only restaurant projects, clients are coming in with booths already on the brief, more as a starting point than an afterthought,” says Sarita Posada, whose eponymous New York City-based design firm is behind some of the hottest tables in Paris and London, including the aforementioned Supernova, as well as Cherry and 74 Duke. “I think people are a little fatigued overall on overexposure, whether that be digitally or when they go out,” she adds, citing booths as a way to carve out your own piece of real estate in a room.

It wasn’t all that long ago that communal tables reigned supreme as the seating setup du jour. David Prior, founder of the editorial-led travel company Prior, cites the farm-to-table movement and food leaders like Alice Waters as popularizing long communal tables roughly from 2009 to 2016. He also points to Jim Denevan’s beloved roving dinner series, Outstanding in the Field, which became famous for its extremely long dinner tables.

But this all changed in 2020, when the pandemic transformed how people ate and gathered. During that period—and the 18 months that followed—private dining became the default. “People wanted to be hermetically sealed,” says Prior with a laugh.

Sleek leather booths at Le Cafe Nac in London, designed by Sarita Posada Interiors.

Now, Prior says that he’s seeing what he calls an “alone-together moment,” and booth seating sits perfectly within that larger movement. “We want to have our intimate moments, but we also want to feel that we’re part of a similar thing,” he says, citing his recent launch party for his podcast, Traveling Through, where groups of people clustered in booths like small islands within a greater archipelago. “It’s all about connection right now, because people are so disconnected.”

Red leather booths at Bar Primi Penn District, designed by Meyer Davis.

Cafe Zaffri, the stylish Mediterranean restaurant within The Twenty Two members’ club in Union Square, is one such setting known to welcome the power lunch crowd in its sumptuous horseshoe booths. “People still want to experience the energy of a lively dining room, but they also want space for real conversation and connection,” says Leigh Salem, a partner at Post Company, whose firm designed the space.

Velvet booths at Cafe Zaffri, inside the New York outpost of The Twenty Two.

From a design perspective, booths also add a sense of storiedness to a space. “There’s something about the memory and history they carry in great, old rooms like Bemelmans Bar or Minetta Tavern,” says Posada, who installed booths in two of her recent restaurant projects to infuse the rooms with intimacy and nostalgia.

But today’s booths are adding a modern twist. At Supernova, Posada drew inspiration from 1970s American diners but made the space cinematic with careful restraint on color—keeping to chrome, black, and butter yellow. In Auric Room 1915, the members-only supper club and speakeasy at Lone Mountain Ranch in Big Sky, cowhide booths bring levity to the space while staying entirely on brand. And how could one miss the chocolate-brown banquettes at Marcel in the iconic Breuer building that made the rounds on Instagram with its buzzy opening?

A ’70s twist on the booth at Supernova in London, designed by Sarita Posada Interiors.

More than just contributing to a feeling, booths add functionality. At the beloved West Village institution Demo, booths were “one of the best ways to utilize a narrow pathway,” says co-owner Jacob Nass. In Bufon, the team’s second restaurant, the perimeter of the dining room is lined with blue banquettes, creating an almost conversation-pit feel.

While booths might look simple, designing one is more technical than one might think. Davis notes it’s important to consider how seating supports different dining durations, service styles, and group sizes and says that the firm carefully evaluates material durability, placement, and seat height when installing a booth. “We use a range of booth typologies which include perimeter banquettes that define a room’s edge, curved or semi-enclosed booths, and integrated seating that becomes part of the architectural millwork.” All of this is in service of supporting the overall design concept.

Outdoor booths are a key feature of the Tatjana von Stein–designed Hotel Corazon in Mallorca.

Booths work in the most serious and stately of spaces, as well as the most fun. Hotel Corazon, the beloved Mallorca hotel run by fashion photographer Kate Bellm and her husband, artist Edgar Lopez, installed bespoke round booths last spring in its revamped restaurant. “The intention was to create a space that feels intimate, warm, and relaxed, while retaining a sense of playfulness,” says designer Tatjana von Stein, who brought the space to life with circular booths crafted from powder-coated metal and made in Portugal with the hotel’s sun motif. “We wanted guests to feel comfortable lingering, connecting, and enjoying the convivial spirit that sits at the heart of Hotel Corazon.”

At One4One, the chic sports bar opened by Dylan Hales and Ronnie Flynn, booths are part of the owners’ broader mission to “create a true local hang.” At The Flower Shop, their first foray into hospitality, there’s a brass plaque above the corner booth that reads “Captain’s Quarters,” reserving it for friends and family.

The expansive, warmly lit booths at One4One.

As you might imagine, securing one of the highly sought-after seats at One4One or The Flower Shop isn’t something the owners take lightly. “A booth creates comfort and, in a way, commitment. You get a booth when you mean it. When you’re settling in for the night, waiting for more people to join, and really planting your flag in a place,” says Flynn. “That is, if you’re lucky enough to snag one.”

#6661. The Launch: November’s Must-Know Fashion News

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Fall is in full swing, and with it, so is the fashion industry. As the leaves continue to turn and preparations for the holiday season get serious, brands are finding new ways to celebrate with exciting new capsules, collaborations, and stocking-worthy releases. Look no further than J.J. Martin, whose new book, Table Energy, explores the art of Italian entertaining, and Rimowa x Maison Margiela, which turns travel into something even more desirable. Below, all the fashion news to know this month.

What: High jewelry collection and new boutique

Where: 237 Worth Ave, Palm Beach, Florida

Why: A 1920s Palm Beach estate is a fitting setting for Bulgari’s first U.S. presentation of “Eclettica.” Designed by Addison Mizner, the waterfront home hosted a gala that also marked the opening of the house’s new boutique. Venus Williams, Chanel Iman, and Becca Bloom were among the guests, with Jewel performing. The collection includes 15 transformable designs—the most Bulgari has presented in a single collection—alongside more than 50 high jewelry pieces. With its Roman roots and sculptural approach to high jewelry, Bulgari’s “Eclettica” brings a distinctly Italian point of view to Palm Beach.

Where: Online at rimowa.com and maisonmargiela.com and select Rimowa and Maison Margiela stores

Why: Some things look better after they’ve been lived in. That idea is at the heart of Rimowa and Maison Margiela’s new travel collaboration, which brings together two signatures: the German luggage house’s familiar grooves and Margiela’s hand-painted white Bianchetto finish. Designed to change with use, the suitcase and matching bag will take on marks and patina as they travel. A campaign by Dexter Lander brings that idea to life in a Haussmannian apartment, where the white paint seems to spill beyond the pieces themselves.

What: Bird on a Rock installation, window displays, and holiday décor

Where: The Landmark; 727 5th Ave, New York City

Why: Tiffany & Co. has switched on the holiday season at The Landmark, with Amanda Seyfried leading the way. The actress lit the flagship’s Bird on a Rock installation by placing an ornament on its Blue Box tree, marking the third year of the display and a full-circle moment. Seyfried stars in the house’s new holiday film, “You & Me,” which travels between present-day New York and a memory from the ’90s. Mikey Madison, Jordyn Woods, and Louisa Jacobson joined the celebration.

Tiffany & Co. Bird on a Rock Wings Narrow Ring

Why: Just in time for the holidays, La DoubleJ founder J.J. Martin has released Table Energy, a new book about the art of Italian entertaining, with a foreword by fashion writer Leandra Medine Cohen. Its pages move from alfresco lunches to candlelit dinners, all in the colorful, convivial spirit of La DoubleJ. The book made its debut at the brand’s Upper East Side boutique, The Lighthouse, where Martin, ELLE Decor’s head of editorial content Elisa Lipsky-Karasz, and ELLE editor-in-chief Nina Garcia gathered to celebrate l’art de la table.

Where: Online at tecovas.com, aninebing.com, and select retail locations

Why: Anine Bing has a new way to kick up a look. The designer has teamed up with Tecovas on a capsule that reworks the label’s Loretta and Jamie boots with star embroidery and polished goat leather. Cowboy hats and belts round out the lineup, which launches alongside Anine Bing’s spring/summer 2027 collection.

#6659. Drew Barrymore Winks to Her 2000s Style in a Black Newsboy Cap

Anyone else thinking of that scene from Charlie’s Angels: Full Throttle?

Last night, the Museum of Modern Art held its annual film benefit in tandem with Chanel, which raises money for “the acquisition and preservation of key film works” in the MoMA’s movie department, with director Steven Spielberg serving as this year’s special honoree. Typically, the New York City event unites some of the starriest names in Hollywood, and the 2026 benefit was no exception, with attendees including the likes of Cate Blanchett, Zoe Saldaña, Emily Blunt, and Michelle Pfeiffer. But even at such an A-list event, one person managed to steal the show: Drew Barrymore.

The talk show host turned heads in a striking, Mod-inspired look, the star of which was a shaggy black-and-white jacket. Meanwhile, her choice of headwear injected the evening with a welcome dose of nostalgia.

Like most of the attendees, Barrymore dressed in Chanel for the occasion, pulling a statement piece of outerwear from the house’s Pre-Fall 2026 collection by Matthieu Blazy. The jacket featured a black-and-white windowpane pattern in a distorted tweed, with fringe tufts running all along the trim. Meanwhile, the lining featured a pattern of repeating faces in red and white, which only peeked out in brief moments.

Stylist Lee Harris left the jacket open to reveal a black turtleneck top and matching slacks underneath, while a long pearl necklace adorned with the house’s signature double-C pendant dangled in front.

However, it was Barrymore’s black newsboy cap that made the greatest statement. Over the years, the Emmy Award-winner has been a champion of all kinds of hat styles, from fedoras and beanies to baseball caps and berets. But you might recall that she went through a strong newsboy-cap phase in the early 2000s, especially when she was promoting the Charlie’s Angels films.

In fact, she event wears one during one of the most-memorable scenes in the sequel, Charlie’s Angels: Full Throttle (2003), when she and co-stars Cameron Diaz and Lucy Liu have an impromptu dance break to MC Hammer’s “U Can’t Touch This.” (You can revisit that incredible moment here.)

In honor of Barrymore, and in honor of cinema, it might just be about time for a rewatch.

#6658. 26 Best Men's Scarves 2026, According to GQ Editors

Are any accessories as essential, yet mysteriously overlooked, as the best men's scarves? First, they warm your neck (and face, and chest) like nothing else. Second, they put a style-forward, cheery, colorful bow on pretty much any outfit. And yet, these soft little miracles are all too often an afterthought in the menswear world. Even if you’re the type of guy to painstakingly lay your fits out the night before, chances are when it comes to your scarf game, you’re still reaching for one you picked up in a rushed pinch from Nordstrom Rack, or at a frigid college football game.

This is, of course, fine. But it’s also sort of a tragedy. Because when you pick up a truly great scarf, everything changes. Swaddling your neck in cashmere (or cashmere-emulating fabrics) doesn’t just provide a soothing all-day embrace through bracing winds. It also, like a necktie, creates an opportunity for a flash of personal style, right under your handsome face. Even better, because scarves use less fabric than coats and knitwear, they’re also a great way to own some of the best materials in our industry for far less scratch.

To help you pick the one you’ll soon be recognized by, I surveyed hundreds of scarves from across the fashion (and budget) spectrum, journeying from mall chains, to historic British manufacturers, to the buzziest makers today, and everything in-between. Below, the final 26 best men's scarves to knot up this winter—and next winter, and the one after that.

Parisian label Brut puts a Big Apple spin on the classic European football supporter scarf, featuring none other than Lady Liberty herself. A fitting French connection.

The bandana, neckerchief, foulard, whatever you want to call it has become an easy, even trendy winter accessory. Alex Mill’s is made from extra-fine merino wool, comes in 14 colors, and costs less than a hundo.

Another bandana-shaped style from the Banana, this time with a generous helping of cashmere for a little extra softness.

A smart tartan plaid as classic as the linings inside Barbour’s famous wax jackets, in a soft wool-cashmere blend. About as British as a rainy afternoon and a pint at the pub.

We cross the Irish Sea for L.L.Bean’s take, made from Irish-woven lambswool, known for its durability and natural water resistance. Plenty warm and handsome to boot.

Lost & Found’s Scottish lambswool scarf comes with pockets stitched into it. Perfect for stashing your cards, cash or other things a little less above board. We won’t ask.

On the GORP-ier side of things, this thermal fleece scarf balances warmth, stretch and lightweight comfort in a slimmed-down design that will both fit with your puffer and stay out of your way.

Quince has made a name for itself selling luxury materials at un-luxury prices. Case in point: this soft scarf made from 100% Mongolian cashmere, at a price you could get two with.

Another triangle scarf, here in a stunning sienna color that’s still right in Margaret Howell’s wheelhouse. Snug and sensible.

Lil’ brown checks, a fuzzy brushed finish, and Japanese cotton-wool twill woven in England. A big helping of understated charm.

A nice change of pace from the usual winter plaids, two-tone chevrons give this Coach scarf a little graphic punch, while a lightweight but warm alpaca blend keeps things cosy.

If you love pattern, fall and winter is primed for Polo Power. This Fair-Isle-esque design is easier to wear than the classic sweater, and will add some energy to your winter fits.

True to form, Kapital keeps things weird with a wild leopard-and-paisley design. The lightweight gauze also means you can wear it a dozen different ways, pretty much any time of year.

William Lockie’s scarves will set you back a few extra bucks, but they’ve been at it since 1874, so you're buying proven scarf smarts. In this case: Pure cashmere, traditional techniques, and even a pre-sale bath in local fresh water for added softness.

Todd Snyder isn’t reinventing the wheel here, this is just a beautifully brushed cashmere scarf. Classic, timeless, soft, and warm as they come.

Howlin’ often brings a little irreverence to its sweaters, and the same goes for its scarves. Here, throwback collegiate “fun” stripes show the brand’s take on the Ivy scarves of yesteryear.

Made from Italian wool, this Mfpen number gives you two checks for the price of one, thanks to a clever double-faced design. Twist it, drape it, wear it however you please.

All the cozy, old-school charm of an Aran knit, Percival takes the classic cream cable-knit sweater and turns it into a scarf. And at more than half off, it’s a bit of a steal.

She's pricey, but you’re paying for fine Scottish-spun cashmere materials and serious know-how with an entirely handmade and hand-linked scarf.

Printed scarves were the first things Drake’s made back in 1977, when it was still a small workshop. These archival designs are works of art you can wear. Wool, silk and good taste.

Missoni’s famous zigzags came out of swinging ’60s Milan, and they still have that groovy Italian charm. Funny how something so unmistakably of its time never seems to go out of style.

A statement scarf if there ever was one, with vibrant Yves Klein blue and an oversized logo patch that’s not shy about announcing itself. A lot to spend on yourself, maybe, but one hell of a gift.

There’s something dashingly medieval about a shearling scarf. Wrap it around your neck for a bit of Feudal-Lord-core. Beats a suit of armor.

NN07 mixes two old-school patterns into one elegant Italian-woven scarf, with a fuzzy brushed finish and blanket-stitched edges. Your granddad would approve.

This fashion-guy-approved cashmere scarf from Auralee is classic enough, but boy, those rich colours are doing something for me. It truly is all in the details.

By now, you may have noticed the Scots know a thing or two about wool. Johnstons of Elgin has been at it for centuries, and this beautifully woven cashmere scarf is further proof.

#6657. Rihanna’s Son Riot Made His Magazine Cover Debut—and She Shared All 6 Versions

Rihanna and A$AP Rocky’s three children are now all magazine cover stars. After their oldest, RZA, made his British Vogue cover debut in 2023 and youngest, Rocki, appeared on two covers this year, middle child Riot Rose is having his turn. The 3-year-old covered Arena Homme+ all on his own, though Rihanna joined him for one shot, wearing the red Loewe jumpsuit she had on when she revealed her pregnancy with him at the 2023 Super Bowl. There are six different versions of his cover, and his proud mother shared every image.

Last month, Rocky hinted at Riot’s cover in an interview with The Cut. He told the outlet, “One of my sons has a modeling gig in like three days, you know, the day before my birthday, and it’s—I’m so proud of him; this is his first magazine cover, so I think it’s just fascinating to see these little people grow into personalities of their own. It’s trippy, just in retrospect, thinking back when they were just so small and little. I mean, they’re still relatively little and small, but you know, they kind of speak up for themselves and have their own kind of swag and shit. It’s crazy.”

While RZA and Rocki posed with their parents, Riot’s cover was all about him. Rihanna teased he was a lot like her in her 2025 interview with Harper’s Bazaar.

“Riot, he’s just hilarious,” she said. “When he wakes up, he starts to squeal, scream. Not in a crying way. He just wants to sing. And I’m like, ‘Okay, here we go!’ He’s my alarm in the morning! He’s not taking no for an answer from anyone. I don’t know where he came from, dude.”

She added that Riot’s big brother, RZA, at first struggled with losing his only-child status “like all [new] siblings do, and at first Riot was understanding that his role was being the little brother. Now he knows he’s in charge.”

#6654. Léa Seydoux Isn’t Trying to Act. She’s Trying to Live

The French actress continues her string of emotionally demanding roles in The Unknown and Gentle Monster

Léa Seydoux first stepped into the limelight in Christophe Honoré’s The Beautiful Person, where her role as Junie de Chartres earned her the Trophée Chopard award for rising actors at Cannes. From there, she moved seamlessly between highbrow French cinema and Hollywood, achieving a critical breakthrough with Blue Is the Warmest Color in 2013 and starring alongside Daniel Craig as a Bond girl in Spectre and No Time to Die. Most years, she’s starred in at least two films, and 2026 is no exception: She plays a woman with a man’s soul trapped in her body in Arthur Harari’s psychological fantasy The Unknown, and in Marie Kreutzer’s Gentle Monster, releasing on Netflix on November 18, she’s a pianist who unearths her husband’s hideous crimes. The words thorny and barbed read like understatements for both films, and it’s exactly what interests Seydoux about the stories. Like in life itself, she avoids easy answers, opting instead for exploration.

Seydoux got the chance to explore an especially ambitious idea in The Unknown. It tells the story of David Zimmerman (Niels Schneider), a photographer who wakes up in the body of a woman he sleeps with. Seydoux plays both that woman, Eva, and the man trapped within her body. “I felt the movie was something new to me, to play an impossible idea and make it believable, try to give it a truthful dimension,” Seydoux says. She’s no stranger to high-concept stories, previously starring in Bertrand Bonello’s The Beast and David Cronenberg’s Crimes of the Future. Each time, she imbues these characters with humanity, despite their far-fetched sci-fi dilemmas.

“I like movies that make you think, movies that bring up questions, when there’s a debate around the film,” she says. “What I love the most is to explore human nature, our human condition. This is what cinema allows us to do.”

Seydoux might vehemently love movies, yet acting remains a demanding process for her. She relies on the art form to dig into feelings and emotions. “I don’t feel necessarily very comfortable with acting. It’s not a place where I’m like, ‘I love it,’ but at the same time, I find it a bit painful. It’s more a way to experience things and ideas,” she says.

Gentle Monster provides another knotty premise, this time grounded in reality. It follows Lucy Weiss, a famed experimental pianist who gives up her career to raise her young son with her doting husband, Philip (Laurence Rupp). One day, the police knock on their door, and it’s revealed that Philip is accused of distributing child pornography.

“The subject matter is tough, but the fact that it’s through the woman’s perspective—and not through the victim or perpetrator—it’s through her emotions that the story unfolds [is what interested me],” she says. “Things are not too defined, but it’s also because of the subject matter; it was the only way to talk about it. [Marie] gave me a lot of freedom.”

Born in Paris in 1985, Seydoux spent her childhood wedged among seven siblings and half-siblings. She remembers feeling isolated, practically invisible, as a child. “I was always in the shadows in a way,” she says. “As a kid, I felt transparent. I was never at the center of [my] big family.” This plays a big part in her surprise at her acting career, never thinking of herself as someone deserving of center stage, of fame, of attention. In fact, acting never even crossed her mind until she befriended some actors when she turned 18. “I loved the way they lived their lives,” she says. “I admired their life—the fact that they were free.”

And yet, she rejects the label of “actress.” “I try to be truthful as much as possible,” she says. “I try not to act. This is what I try to be, and I’m more into reaction than action.” She adds, “It’s more reactive than acting.”

For Seydoux, “reacting” and really experiencing life is only possible if she “abandons” herself to her characters. One of the most intense examples of this is Abdellatif Kechiche’s controversial lesbian love story Blue Is the Warmest Color, in which she stars alongside Adèle Exarchopoulos. The film’s schedule stretched from two months to five months, and it has since become notorious for its grueling pace. (The famous sex scene took 10 days alone.) “The greatest and most intense experience I’ve had was with Adèle when we did Blue Is the Warmest Color,” she recalls. “It was crazy, and really the connection between us had to be very, very intense. I think, with Adèle, it’s something that will always be a part of me now. There was an exchange, and it was more than making a film. It was really a life experience.”

One scene from Gentle Monster lingered with me for weeks after I watched it: Lucy’s snotty, tearful confrontation with her husband at their family home as she pleads with him to tell the truth. This close-up of Seydoux not only accentuates her famous blue eyes but also shows her uncanny control of this character’s emotions. It feels, for lack of better words, real. Seydoux partly credits her empathy to being a mother of two children, but this scene goes beyond compassion; it shows how much of herself she gives to the character. Before filming this scene, Kreutzer offered little direction, letting her tap into how the character felt. “I prepare myself, and I have to just let myself go and be in the moment and just open up,” Seydoux says, suggesting that perhaps these emotions otherwise lie dormant within her.

I found this is what Seydoux means by “reaction.” Every role in her varied and extolled filmography functions as an avenue through which she can explore what it means to be human, what it means to feel. Her natural curiosity about the world and its inhabitants existed before she decided to act in her teens and will exist long into the future, even if acting jobs don’t remain on the table. “If it ended tomorrow, I’d be happy,” she says. “I will find a way. Now, I really feel that I’m acting because I still have the opportunity. But I have more things to explore, and I would love to have more experiences.”
